newsitem.title: USA: Lilco merger plan boosts debt, spreads firm.
newsitem.headline: Lilco merger plan boosts debt, spreads firm.

text.p: Long Island Lighting Co's (LILCO) debt restructuring plans got a boost on Monday from the company's proposed merger with Brooklyn Union Gas Co, traders and analysts said.

Spreads of outstanding LILCO debt to comparable U.S. Treasuries tightened 15 to 20 basis points on the bid side across the curve, traders said. Commerce will likely remain elusive until all details of the deal and any debt manipulations evolve, they added.
"We still have to see what they do with the debt but the deal is viewed favorable for LILCO bondholders," said Tom Mockler, vice president and analyst at Dillon Read & Co Inc.
No markets were seen for Brooklyn Union debt, but traders said any quotes were sure to be slightly weaker.

The two utilities on Sunday said they agreed to merge in a tax-free stock deal that would create a $4.0 billion electric and gas holding company. The companies also said they will continue talks with the Long Island Power Authority (LIPA) that may lead to the agency's assumption and refinancing of $4.5 billion in LILCO debt via less-costly tax-exempt bonds.
The debt is associated with LILCO's Shoreham nuclear power plant, which never opened.

Brooklyn Union Gas, far less levered than LILCO, was viewed negatively by association by major rating agencies. The company in a conference call on Monday expressed committment to the deal with no contingencies, however, suggesting a deal for the refinancing of LILCO's massive debt load is in the offing, said Tom Chistolini, senior securities analyst at Conseco Capital Management Inc.
"They must be pretty confident that something will happen with Shoreham," Chistolini said. "I think they feel petty good either LIPA or securitization will come to fruition."

The two companies said LIPA would make an announcement of a transaction within the next four to six weeks, according to utility analysts who participated in a conference call with the two entities on Monday morning. The companies would not elaborate further, Chistolini said.
Calls to LILCO Chairman William Catacosinos and Brooklyn Union Gas Chairman Robert Catell were not returned.
Favorable comments from the New York State Governor George Pataki and LIPA chairman Frank Zarb also bolstered beliefs that the deal would be consummated, debt analysts said.
"This is the first transaction that's been out there that's been endorsed by LILCO," Chistolini said. "This is a company-backed plan, so there's some credibility."
Mockler said LILCO is more anxious to refinance their higher couponed mortgage bonds to cut costs. But a refinancing remains unclear with myriad possibilities for execution, he said.
"One possibility is that LIPA buys something and refinances it for tax-exempts and another is that they buy something and give LILCO some cash and LILCO calls the bonds," Mocker said.
On the flip side, Mockler said a breakdown between LILCO and LIPA may result in a more hostile political tone and cause the markets to trade off.
He added: "It also depends on what the (Internal Revenue Service) says and the appetite of all parties to come to an agreement."
Standard & Poor's on Monday said it may raise its ratings of LILCO's debt and/or lower those of Brooklyn Union Gas.
Moody's Investors Service said it revised its outlook on LILCO debt to positive from stable and that it may cut Brooklyn Union's ratings.
